items.title: Windows 11 collects data on usage of coding agents and developer tools via MissionControlAggregator.dll, reporting to Microsoft Diagnostics by default [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Windows 11 Is Collecting Data on Which Coding Agents and Developer Tools You Use
items.summary:
Windows 11 includes a system component, MissionControlAggregator.dll, that tracks which coding agents like copilot.exe and developer tools such as python.exe and gcc.exe are used on the system. This data is collected by monitoring Windows events related to application activity and is saved locally before being uploaded to Microsoft Diagnostics unless users opt out of optional diagnostic data collection.

The component categorizes tools into groups including CLI agents and desktop agents, verifying some publishers like Microsoft Corporation and Python Software Foundation. It reports usage through Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) by sending bitmaps indicating which tools were observed during a reporting window, without detailed usage metrics. This telemetry is embedded in Windows 11 binaries and operates by subscribing to existing system events rather than scanning processes directly.

items.title: OpenCode launches Browse, a Chromium extension and MCP server enabling AI agents to use users' real browsers with tabs, logins, and extensions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenCode Browse
items.summary:
OpenCode has released Browse, a tool combining an MCP server and a Chromium extension that allows AI agents to operate within users' real browsers, including Chrome, Edge, Brave, and others. The agents can open tabs in the background, interact with pages by clicking and typing, take screenshots, and record tabs, while handing control back to users for sensitive actions like logins, two-factor authentication, or payments.

Browse supports multiple MCP clients such as OpenCode, Claude Code, and Cursor, and uses the user's existing logged-in sessions without requiring additional setup or keys. Users can also lend tabs to agents and restrict agent activity to specified sites. Installation is guided through the Chrome extension, with additional command-line options available. OpenCode also offers related products including Hex for voice dictation, OpenTunnel for public HTTPS URLs, and OpenTUI for terminal user interfaces.

items.title: Developer builds lend tool to let remote coding agents use laptop credentials with user approval, avoiding credential exposure [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Running coding agents without handing them my credentials
items.summary:
A developer created lend, a proxy tool that allows remote coding agents running on disposable VMs to access tools and credentials on their laptop without exposing sensitive data. The tool forwards requests through an SSH agent extension, requiring user approval via biometric authentication before executing commands or signing requests locally.

The developer uses herdr, a terminal multiplexer for managing multiple coding agents, and Ovis, a client for interacting with agents remotely via chat-like interfaces. Lend enforces a policy on the laptop that restricts what commands and keys the remote agents can use, ensuring credentials like SSH keys and API tokens never leave the laptop. This approach addresses common security issues with copying credentials to VMs or forwarding SSH agents without control.

By keeping credentials on the laptop and requiring explicit approval for each request, lend enhances security while enabling flexible remote agent workflows. The developer's setup supports running multiple AI coding agents in parallel on VMs while maintaining control over sensitive authentication materials.

items.summary: Users on Hacker News discuss how the growing demand for AI workloads is driving up the cost of virtual private servers (VPS), making it harder to find affordable options for small web projects. One user noted that their $10 VPS with 4 vCPUs, 8GB RAM, and 75GB NVMe storage is now the best they can get unless prices change. The community expresses frustration over justifying higher VPS prices as AI consumes more computing resources, potentially making hobby and small-scale projects more expensive to maintain.

items.title: Analysis finds large language models struggle to design AI systems effectively, often choosing flawed symbolic approaches over LLM-based solutions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LLMs are terrible at designing AI systems
items.summary:
A recent analysis highlights that large language models (LLMs) frequently fail when tasked with designing AI systems, often opting for complex symbolic methods rather than leveraging LLM capabilities. Despite their proficiency in writing standard code, LLMs tend to misapply tools when addressing AI-specific problems, leading to ineffective designs.

The discussion cites examples where LLMs attempted to solve tasks like contradiction detection using symbolic logic solvers instead of simpler LLM calls, resulting in dead-end solutions. Possible reasons include outdated training data, reinforcement learning environments lacking LLM-to-LLM interaction, and inherent limitations in AI agents' software design skills. This suggests that while LLMs excel in many areas, their software design abilities remain inconsistent and require careful human oversight.

items.title: Researchers analyze memory filtering in LLM agents, showing that hard deletion of stale facts can reduce accuracy when query-critical facts are mistakenly removed [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Should LLM Agents Forget? Memory Filtering Under Query-Critical Resolver Errors
items.summary: This study examines how large language model (LLM) memory systems that delete facts deemed stale can suffer accuracy losses if resolver errors cause removal of query-critical information. Experiments across three models reveal that sensitivity adjustments to hard-filtering can shift outcomes from accuracy gains at perfect resolution to significant losses at low reliability. The research highlights that false deletions degrade performance more than false retentions, and that non-deleting baselines may still fail if incorrect labels influence generation. A deployment-matched gating approach improves accuracy compared to always deleting stale facts, but optimal deletion strategies depend on task-specific diagnostics and availability of validation data. The authors recommend treating deletion as a cost-sensitive decision, validating risks on matched data or defaulting to retention when validation is unavailable.
items.description: This study examines how large language model (LLM) memory systems that delete facts deemed stale can suffer accuracy losses if resolver errors cause removal of query-critical information. Experiments across three models reveal that sensitivity adjustments to hard-filtering can shift outcomes from accuracy gains at perfect resolution to significant losses at low reliability. The research highlights that false deletions degrade performance more than false retentions, and that non-deleting baselines may still fail if incorrect labels influence generation. A deployment-matched gating approach improves accuracy compared to always deleting stale facts, but optimal deletion strategies depend on task-specific diagnostics and availability of validation data. The authors recommend treating deletion as a cost-sensitive decision, validating risks on matched data or defaulting to retention when validation is unavailable.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are model- and task-specific diagnostics, not deployment thresholds. Deletion should instead be treated as cost-sensitive: validate query-critical false-drop risk on matched data, or default to label-free retention when such validation is unavailable.

items.title: Audit finds hallucination detector rankings invert between small, quantized on-device LLMs, with lexical baseline matching sampling-based methods on TriviaQA [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Does the Ranking Hold? A Practitioner-Facing Audit of Hallucination Detectors on Small, Quantized, On-Device LLMs
items.summary: Researchers conducted a reproducible audit of four hallucination detectors across two small, instruction-tuned language models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) loaded at 4-bit quantization on a single GPU, evaluating performance on closed-book TriviaQA. They found poor cross-model ranking transfer, with detector rankings inverting between models and the simple lexical baseline performing comparably to more complex sampling-based consistency detectors. The study also identified that standard token-overlap correctness labeling for TruthfulQA-Generation yields near-chance detector performance, indicating labeler issues rather than detector failures.
items.description: Researchers conducted a reproducible audit of four hallucination detectors across two small, instruction-tuned language models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) loaded at 4-bit quantization on a single GPU, evaluating performance on closed-book TriviaQA. They found poor cross-model ranking transfer, with detector rankings inverting between models and the simple lexical baseline performing comparably to more complex sampling-based consistency detectors. The study also identified that standard token-overlap correctness labeling for TruthfulQA-Generation yields near-chance detector performance, indicating labeler issues rather than detector failures.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17339v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hallucination detection for large language models is dominated by methods evaluated on 7B-70B research models with abundant sampling budgets and exact-match or ROUGE correctness labels. The small models practitioners actually ship on-device, Phi-3-mini, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-2B-Instruct, typically at 4-bit precision, sit outside this evidence base. We present a reproducible one-GPU audit of four detectors spanning three paradigms: length-normalized token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, and two sampling-based consistency methods (semantic entropy and SelfCheckGPT-NLI) on two small open instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) loaded at 4-bit NF4 quantization on a single Colab T4 GPU, evaluated on closed-book TriviaQA. Cross-model ranking transfer is poor: Spearman rho is -0.80 and Kendall tau-b is -0.667, meaning the detector ranking actively inverts between the two models, and the cheap lexical baseline is statistically indistinguishable from the sampling-based consistency detectors on both models under bootstrap 95 percent confidence intervals. As a second, methodological contribution, we show that the standard token-overlap-to-multiple-choice correctness labeler for TruthfulQA-Generation produces near-chance AUROC (0.46-0.59) for all four detectors on both models, a labeler failure, not a detector failure, since the same detectors reach 0.69-0.89 AUROC on TriviaQA under the identical pipeline. We release the harness, prompts, and per-item scores and frame the detector choice explicitly as a fairness-of-error-rates allocation problem for practitioners deploying on resource-constrained, on-device hardware.

items.title: LoRAWeaver introduces training-free adapter routing by aligning LoRA adapter outputs with task prototypes using cosine similarity, improving selection in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LoRAWeaver: Directional Adapter Routing in LoRA Representation Space
items.summary: LoRAWeaver proposes a training-free method for routing task-specific LoRA adapters in large language models by treating adapter selection as a representation alignment problem in the adapter-output space. The method matches adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes using cosine similarity, avoiding retraining when new adapters are added and simplifying inference in dynamic settings. Experiments with LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B on a 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark and out-of-distribution tasks show that LoRAWeaver outperforms other training-free baselines and approaches the performance of trained retrieval encoders. An ablation study confirms the advantage of directional alignment in the adapter-output space for effective adapter routing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are expensive to update through full retraining. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adaptation, but repeated adaptation creates a growing pool of task-specific LoRA adapters. This pool complicates adapter selection during inference. Existing routing and encoder-based methods often require retraining when new adapters are added, which limits their use in dynamic settings. This paper treats adapter routing as a representation alignment problem in the adapter-output space. The proposed training-free method selects adapters by matching adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes using cosine similarity. Experiments with LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B on a 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark and on out-of-distribution tasks show that the method outperforms training-free baselines in the cross-task setting and approaches a trained retrieval encoder without learning a router. An ablation confirms the benefit of directional alignment in the adapter-output space.

items.title: Researchers propose tabular population priors for EHR medication set prediction, improving F1 score by 11.5% over patient-level retrieval on MIMIC IV data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Tabular Population Priors as Structured Retrieval for EHR Medication Set Prediction
items.summary:
Researchers introduce a method using tabular population priors derived from condition-medication co-occurrence tables to improve medication prediction from electronic health records (EHR). This approach replaces patient-level retrieval in a clinical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system, resulting in an 11.5% relative increase in F1 score and improved Jaccard index on 1,004 held-out MIMIC IV admissions without additional large language model (LLM) calls or inference-time patient indexing.

The study demonstrates that aggregate population statistics offer a more task-aligned, efficient, and auditable retrieval source than nearest-neighbor patient retrieval for fixed vocabulary EHR medication set prediction. A non-LLM baseline confirms the predictive value of the population prior before integration with LLMs, suggesting potential for more streamlined clinical AI workflows.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medication prediction from electronic health records is a fixed vocabulary structured prediction problem, yet recent clinical RAG systems often treat it like open ended case based reasoning: retrieve similar patient admissions and ask an LLM to infer a medication set. This retrieval object is indirect the model receives retrieved patient records while the target is a discrete set of medication class labels. We propose a more task aligned retrieval object: a tabular population prior ranked medication class candidates from a sparse condition medication co occurrence table estimated from training admissions. Using PACERAG as a fixed downstream pipeline and replacing only its patient retriever, this drop in swap improves F1 from 0.303 to 0.338 (+11.5% relative) and Jaccard from 0.218 to 0.237 on 1,004 heldout MIMIC IV admissions, with no additional LLM calls and no inference time patient index. A non LLM top k baseline reaches F1=0.248, confirming the prior is predictive before LLM integration. Aggregate population statistics can provide a more task aligned, efficient, and auditable retrieval source than patient level nearest neighbors for fixed vocabulary EHR set prediction.

items.title: Researchers operationalize a measure of opaque serial depth in AI models to assess unverbalized serial cognition and propose tracking NLS depth alongside chain-of-thought monitorability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth
items.summary:
Researchers introduce a measure called natural-language-rooted serial (NLS) depth to quantify the longest computation path in AI models that bypasses interpretable bottlenecks, serving as a proxy for unverbalized serial cognition. This measure can be determined before training based on architecture and training configuration and is unaffected by post-training techniques like prompting or distillation.

The study finds that NLS depth correlates strongly with model layer count across open-weight models and has increased slowly over recent years. The researchers analyze how NLS depth applies to various architectures, including standard transformers and latent-reasoning models, and provide an example bounding the depth of the Gemma3-1B model. They recommend that AI developers report NLS depth alongside direct chain-of-thought monitorability metrics to better understand model interpretability.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is currently a valuable tool for overseeing AI models, but some architectural shifts could significantly reduce CoT monitorability. We operationalize a measure that serves as a proxy for the amount of unverbalized serial cognition a model can perform, as a specific instantiation of the notion of opaque serial depth: roughly, the length of the longest path through a model's computation that does not pass through an interpretable bottleneck. Our main contribution is a particular standard for what counts as such a bottleneck. We define natural-language-rooted (NL-rooted) nodes as nodes that were initialized from a pre-training prior to produce human-understandable outputs, whose output space has not been expanded beyond that prior, and whose outputs the model has not been modified to interpret as a different type of data. By construction, the resulting measure, NLS depth, can be adjudicated before training from an architecture, training recipe, and deployment configuration alone, and is insensitive to ordinary post-training such as prompting, distillation, and RL. We find that, across open-weight models, NLS depth correlates strongly with layer count, with some exceptions, and has grown slowly over recent years. It would likely grow slowly under continued scaling of standard transformers, while latent-reasoning architectures such as full-bandwidth transformers could increase it by a large amount. We work through how NLS depth applies to a range of existing and proposed architectures, discuss alternative operationalizations, and give a worked example bounding the depth of Gemma3-1B. We argue that AI developers should track and report the NLS depth of their models as a complement to direct measurements of CoT monitorability.

items.title: Researchers evaluate MXFP8 and 6-bit MXFP6 quantization formats for recommendation and ranking models on AMD MI350X, achieving up to 2x GEMM speedups without quality loss [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats
items.summary:
Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models in digital advertising require high inference throughput but are highly sensitive to precision loss, enforcing a strict quality margin of 0.01% Normalized Entropy compared to FP16 or FP32 baselines. This constraint has limited aggressive quantization adoption in the domain. Researchers present an empirical study of MXFP8 and 6-bit MXFP6 quantization formats on the AMD MI350X architecture, demonstrating significant speedups in GEMM kernel performance while maintaining model quality within the strict threshold.

The study shows that MXFP6, which quantizes both weights and activations to 6-bit elements and computes natively, can selectively improve queries per second (QPS) without breaching quality limits. MXFP8 is also found to be a viable alternative to row-wise FP8 with comparable accuracy, allowing selection of faster kernels per GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, MXFP8 achieved 1.33–1.55x speedups and MXFP6 achieved 1.73–1.99x speedups over FP16 across linear layers, with up to 2.90x on individual layers, resulting in end-to-end inference throughput gains of 1.5–5.3% and 7.6–14.3% for the two models respectively compared to FP8 configurations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold. We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.

items.title: Researchers test framing effects and internal state interventions on Gemma 3 12B LLM agent's collusive behavior in London silver-fixing market simulation
items.originalTitle: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
items.summary: Researchers simulated 260 market interactions placing the Gemma 3 12B large language model as a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, testing how different behavioral economics frames—gain, loss, blame, and credit—affect the agent's willingness to collude on silver prices. They also examined the impact of management pressure and endorsement by another defendant on collusion and trading volume. In initial tests, loss and blame frames significantly increased collusion rates, while management pressure raised trading volume without increasing collusion. In a second phase, injecting internal states induced by these frames into the model reversed some effects: loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant and refuse collusion requests, whereas gain and credit states increased collusion. This study highlights how framing and internal state manipulations can influence LLM agent behavior in simulated market manipulation scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22. In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.

items.title: Researchers propose model annealing to improve data-efficient learning by reviewing and consolidating network knowledge through episodic training and memory averaging [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Model Annealing: Data-Efficient Learning through Review and Consolidation
items.summary: Researchers introduce model annealing, a training method that divides learning into episodes with reheated and cooled learning rates, using a memory of past network states to relearn from labels, tempered predictions, and adversarial examples. This approach improves top-1 accuracy by an average of 1.3 points over cross-entropy training on datasets like CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet across multiple architectures, while enhancing likelihood, calibration, and robustness to corruptions and adversarial perturbations. The method averages predictions rather than weights, allowing the final deployed network to operate without extra inference cost. Model annealing shows consistent benefits for AdamW-trained models but lowers accuracy for an SGD-trained ResNet-18, though it still improves robustness. The study finds that relearning from memory and adversarial "dreams" reduces overconfidence and performance drift seen in snapshot distillation, especially with limited data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A small labelled dataset is memorized long before the training budget runs out, and the one-hot labels that remain to be fitted then mostly sharpen confidence. Model annealing spends the rest of the budget on review and consolidation, relearning from the network's own knowledge. Training is divided into episodes whose learning rate is raised again and cooled, every cooled state joins a memory of past selves, and each new episode learns from the labels, from the tempered predictions of this memory, and from adversarial dreams sought where student and memory disagree most. The memory averages predictions rather than weights, and the deployed network is the last student, so inference costs nothing extra. Across CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet and Imagewoof, four architecture families and 5\% to 100\% of the labels, model annealing raises the top-1 accuracy of the AdamW-trained ConvNeXt, ViT and MLP-Mixer over cross-entropy training in 28 of 33 configurations, by 1.3 points on average, and is on par in accuracy with snapshot distillation, the closest competitor. On these families it is better than both in likelihood, calibration and robustness to corruptions and small adversarial perturbations. For an SGD-trained ResNet-18 it lowers accuracy but still improves robustness to small adversarial perturbations. Separating the reheated schedule from relearning shows that relearning helps every family and that the losses come from reheats, which undo most of this network's fit to its training set. How early the accuracy of a cross-entropy run saturates largely separates the AdamW families from ResNet-18 but does not predict the gain within them. With little data, relearning from the latest snapshot without dreams, as snapshot distillation does, compounds overconfidence in the AdamW families from episode to episode. The memory and the dreams each curb most of this drift, and together they remove it.

items.originalTitle: Astrocyte Biocomputing: Astrocytic Contributions to Neural Network Computation
items.summary: Recent research highlights astrocytes, non-electrical brain cells comprising about 50% of brain cells, as key contributors to cognitive functions like learning and memory. Scientists have developed machine learning algorithms inspired by two astrocyte features: their ability to modulate thousands of synapses simultaneously and their slow, rhythmic communication dynamics. These astrocyte-based models demonstrate faster training, enhanced noise robustness, rapid anomaly detection, and prevention of catastrophic forgetting compared to traditional neuron-focused algorithms. The findings suggest that incorporating astrocyte characteristics can address critical weaknesses in current state-of-the-art machine learning models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17532v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conductors are critical for the performance of an orchestra even though they do not emit sound. Basic research and clinical studies in the last decade are revealing that astrocytes may be the "conductors" of the "orchestra" that is the brain network: astrocytes make up approximately $50\%$ of all brain cells but do not emit electrical signals. Nevertheless, they may play critical roles in important cognitive brain functions, specifically learning, memory, and information processing. Here we consider the implications of these discoveries for brain-inspired machine learning (ML), where analogy is typically drawn between neurons and their electrical interactions. We highlight specific algorithms for two key astrocyte characteristics. The first characteristic is the ability to link to and modulate thousands of synapses simultaneously. A model based on this characteristic yields faster training and makes the network more robust to noise, providing a supervised learning algorithm that can be applied to any existing neural network. The second characteristic we focus on is that the non-electrical communication among astrocytes includes slow, rhythmic dynamics. The rhythmic sharing algorithm we developed based on this premise yields rapid anomaly detection adaptation and prevents catastrophic forgetting. Overall, we find that astrocyte-derived algorithms outperform neurocentric algorithms significantly and remediate critical weaknesses of current state-of-the-art ML models.

items.title: Researchers develop verifiable agentic search method using LLM agents to improve powder X-ray diffraction structure determination, raising recovery rates from 27% to 69% on simulated benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Verifiable pXRD: Hill-climbing pXRD structure determination with LLM agents
items.summary:
Researchers present a verifiable agentic search approach for autonomous crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD), addressing a key bottleneck in self-driving materials laboratories. They introduce pXRD-Bench, a suite of 200 simulated single-phase problems, and demonstrate that agent adaptation improves structural recovery significantly, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided inference-time scaling.

The approach extends to experimental multiphase pXRD through a reflexive evolution framework that learns from self-generated synthetic problems, using an evolver agent to diagnose solver failures and develop guidance and tools for measured patterns. Testing on 15 measured patterns from solid-state synthesis shows improved profile agreement and recovery of phases absent from the reference library, illustrating how learning from verifiable synthetic experience can enhance characterization of experimental samples with unknown structures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) remains a key bottleneck for self-driving materials laboratories. We formulate the task of pXRD structure determination as a verifiable agentic search problem: candidate structures can be assessed during inference through forward-simulated profile agreement and during evaluation through structural matching to a known reference. To benchmark progress, we introduce pXRD-Bench, a suite of 200 simulated single-phase problems spanning in-distribution structure determination, challenging and polymorphic structures, and controlled compositional and topological distribution shifts. Agent adaptation raises selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided inference-time scaling. We extend this approach to experimental multiphase pXRD through a reflexive evolution framework that learns from self-generated synthetic problems. A replaceable laboratory specification defines the sample family and measurement conditions. An evolver agent uses the known generating structures and measurement parameters to diagnose solver failures and develop persistent guidance and executable tools, which are then provided to agents on measured patterns. This supplies verifiable training experience without requiring a collection of solved experimental measurements. On 15 measured patterns from solid-state synthesis, the evolved package improves average profile agreement and transfers an analogue-substitution procedure that recovers a phase whose structure is absent from the supplied reference library. These results demonstrate how learning from verifiable synthetic experience can improve agentic characterization of experimental samples whose structures are not known in advance.

items.title: Researchers introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system enabling human-AI collaboration to understand, contest, and shape AI governance rules using 3,653 government documents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI
items.summary:
AI-Voyager is a system designed to help people and AI work together to interpret and influence the rules governing artificial intelligence. It allows users to access and analyze AI-related regulations from city to national levels, verify statements through agentic search, and propose revisions. The system processed thousands of governance documents and demonstrated strong performance in retrieving relevant information for civic reasoning tasks.

In a study involving 24 participants unfamiliar with two AI bills, users engaged with the system by selecting explanation types and reviewing citations, which helped ground their understanding though rarely prompted source verification. By linking AI assistance directly to official public documents, AI-Voyager establishes a framework for designing tools that support public participation in AI governance and evaluation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.

items.title: Researchers enumerate all representations and action rules in a four-state world to analyze how information retention affects task payoff and cost under various conditions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Does Less Information Pay? An Exact Finite Atlas of Representation, Payoff, and Cost
items.summary:
This study examines how different representations that retain varying amounts of information about a four-state world impact task accuracy and payoff. By enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules, the researchers compare performance across three tasks, their mixtures, and four hypothetical cost tariffs, finding that sometimes less informative representations yield higher payoffs depending on which distinctions are preserved.

The analysis reveals that pairs of representations can have different information amounts but equal task accuracy, and that advantages of lower-information representations depend on the specific distinctions retained. The results provide an exact, complete census of the finite sets of constructions and comparisons, offering a reproducible model to explore how action constraints, counting rules, and cost assumptions influence the relationship between information quantity and decision value.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A representation that retains one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly, while another that retains 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy. The difference lies in which distinctions each representation preserves. We examine this relationship in a uniform four-state world by enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules. Constructions are compared both by replacing one component while holding the others fixed and by choosing the best action rule separately for each module. We consider three tasks, their mixtures, and four separate hypothetical cost tariffs. In some comparisons, the representation retaining less world information has the higher payoff; in others, the more informative representation does. There are also pairs with different information amounts but equal payoff--that is, equal task accuracy. If a representation preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones, its best zero-cost payoff cannot decrease. Lower-information advantages therefore depend on which distinctions are retained. Equal counts of opposing advantages under representation replacement follow from coding symmetry. In broader comparisons, the shares depend on how repeated realizations are counted. A different task set or resource price can change which member of a fixed pair performs better. These results are exact, complete censuses of the specified finite sets of constructions and comparisons. The atlas provides a reproducible worked model for examining how action constraints, counting rules, and cost assumptions affect comparisons. It illustrates established distinctions between information quantity and decision value rather than proposing a new general law of their relation. $I(W;R)$ measures retained world information, and payoff measures task accuracy.

items.title: Researchers analyze 516 multi-agent LLM configurations, finding multi-agent systems often underperform single-pass baselines when controlling for sample count and compute resources [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
items.summary: A study synthesizing nine empirical evaluations of multi-agent language models (LLMs) across 516 configurations finds that multi-agent systems generally do not outperform single-pass baselines when matched for sample count or resource budget. The analysis shows that multi-agent accuracy is equal to or below baseline in 74% of comparable cases, with average accuracy differences remaining negative across sensitivity checks. The researchers note that communication among agents adds no benefit when evidence is identical, suggesting positive gains require partitioned evidence, external verification, or diverse model errors. The study provides a reviewer checklist and tools for accounting resource use in multi-agent LLM evaluations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.

items.originalTitle: LLM-Guided Cluster Lifecycle Management: Deciding When and How to Evolve Behavioral Clusters
items.summary:
Researchers introduce a method using a large language model (LLM) to manage the lifecycle of behavioral clusters derived from user or item interactions, deciding per cluster whether to split, merge, retire, create, or take no action without re-clustering. This approach contrasts with traditional threshold-based triggers and refit-and-track methods, offering a threshold-free, whole-population view that incorporates statistical health, labels, and member texts.

The study evaluates the LLM-guided policy on three public datasets with varying label richness, showing it achieves higher F1 scores with fewer interventions and greater precision than tuned threshold heuristics and a MONIC baseline. The method adapts its signal modality from statistics to semantics depending on label distinctiveness, using a fixed policy and prompt template across datasets, while traditional baselines fail to generalize. The findings highlight the potential of LLMs to provide flexible, data-driven cluster management without hardcoded rules.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Behavioral clusters learned over user or item interactions drift as behavior evolves: some fragment into sub-behaviors, some converge, some disappear, and new patterns emerge. Two paradigms dominate the maintenance of evolving clusterings. Threshold triggers fire a pre-specified action when a hardcoded statistic crosses a cutoff; refit-and-track (MONIC-style) re-clusters every window and infers transitions from how the new clusters align with the previous window's. Both hardwire the decision into a threshold or a re-clustering rule. We study an alternative in which a large language model (LLM) makes the lifecycle decision in place. Given a threshold-free, whole-population view of the current cluster set (statistical health, labels, member texts, residual mass), the LLM decides per cluster whether and how to act (split, merge, retire, create, or no-action) without re-clustering. Because the useful signal channel depends on how informative the labels are, we fix a richness-conditioned policy in advance: statistics when label distinctiveness is low, fused statistics+semantics when it is high. On three public datasets spanning label richness (YooChoose 0.17, MOOC 0.50, News-Category 0.70), the policy-selected LLM mode obtains the highest F1 on all three, with far fewer interventions and stronger restraint than tuned threshold heuristics and a MONIC steelman (paired Wilcoxon p <= 0.003, bootstrap 95% CIs excluding zero). The gain is concentrated more in precision than recall. The useful modality shifts from statistics to semantics/fusion as richness rises. Semantics hurt on YooChoose, fusion is roughly neutral on MOOC, and the semantic channel is required on News. One base prompt template and one fixed policy serve all three datasets, whereas the tuned baseline collapses when moved between them. We treat this shift as a practitioner diagnostic observed on three datasets, not a validated law.

items.title: Researchers audit preventative persona steering in language models, finding it alters refusal behavior and is not safety-neutral across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Safety Side Effects of Preventative Persona Steering: An Empirical Audit
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated preventative persona steering techniques designed to suppress undesirable traits like sycophancy and hallucination in language models by manipulating activation space vectors. They tested three models on safety benchmarks, trait expression, coherence, and Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) accuracy to assess the impact of these methods beyond capability metrics.

The study found that preventative steering changes refusal behavior depending on the trait targeted, challenging prior claims that it is safety-neutral. The authors recommend that steering methods be assessed using multiple safety benchmarks to fully understand their effects on model behavior.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17620v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-level behaviors such as sycophancy and hallucination correspond to directions in a model's activation space (Chen et al., 2025). These directions, known as persona vectors, can suppress undesirable traits either at inference time, subtracting the vector during generation, or through preventative steering, adding the vector during fine-tuning, so the optimizer never needs to encode the trait in weights, then removing the vector at evaluation. Chen et al. (2025) recommend preventative steering because it preserves Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) accuracy, but validations of this recommendation have measured capability alone. We primarily evaluate results on preventative steering of sycophancy and hallucination vectors on three models, measuring three safety benchmarks alongside trait expression, coherence, and MMLU. Our findings show that preventative steering still changes refusal behavior, but by an amount that depends on the trait and does not establish that preventative persona steering is safety-neutral, and steering methods should be evaluated on several safety benchmarks.

items.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.

items.title: Generated Evaluation Suites as Diversity-Driven Search for Real Agent Regressions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Generated Evaluation Suites as Diversity-Driven Search for Real Agent Regressions
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generating an evaluation suite from an agent's specification is diversity-driven search: a generator fills a descriptor space (requirements $\times$ personas $\times$ scenario kinds), and the suite it emits is an archive, then scored like a benchmark by its mean pass rate, which throws away the search's product. We inject 7 controlled defects into a $\tau^2$-bench agent across two domains. Coverage yields a ceiling: if a defect's traced footprint holds $b$ scenarios that pass at baseline, it can itself contribute at most $b/N$ to a suite of $N$. For 4 of 5 traceable defects that ceiling lies at or below the detection threshold $\theta = 0.10$, so no within-footprint effect can move the suite past it; in both domains the tool-removal defect destroys every covered scenario it can (exactly its ceiling) while the suite-level pass rate moves the other way. Defects split into two regimes: trace-aligned ones, where per-cell scoring recovers the tool-removal defect in full and reveals a second as a significant improvement, and trace-orthogonal ones, whose footprint is behavioural: forced escalation is detected in retail at a traced coverage of exactly zero. Diversity along the generator's own axes helps only where it aligns: at fixed suite size a happy-path-only suite detects nothing, while a kind-diverse one detects the orchestration defect in 5 of 20 draws. Evaluation archives should be scored per cell and should publish coverage as a first-class property.

items.title: What LLM Agents See and What Users Say [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: What LLM Agents See and What Users Say
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Before an LLM agent cancels a reservation or deletes a folder for a user, what stops it from acting on a false assumption: what its tools show, or what the user says? In this work, we study this gap with presupposition theory from linguistics: an agent may act only if each claim behind the act (e.g., one reservation fits the name) is seen to hold, answered by the user, or disclosed while the act can be undone. A simple bound shows that when lookups cannot tell one record from two, any agent acts without asking first as often with two records as with one. We then vary whether a search lists, counts, or omits a second match, and whether the user states a claim that a record refutes (e.g., "It is empty"). Under a role-only prompt, a count of a second record leaves most of 36 earlier agents acting on the one they see, whereas listing both stops most. When the user says a record such as a folder is empty, however, a count of its one item stops agents about as often as a listing, and stating the claim mostly cuts acting when it is false. The newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record, then never act. When we add a same-name, same-zip customer to a retail benchmark, a lookup returning that customer first led to wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations, and one that checks a street the user knows kept completion near the one-customer level. Safe writes therefore need lookups that list or check competing records, and evaluations that vary what tools show.

items.title: Learn then Bet: Learning Interpretable Rules for Reliable Agent Intervention [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Learn then Bet: Learning Interpretable Rules for Reliable Agent Intervention
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous agents now run for hundreds of steps with little or no human supervision. In practice, practitioners use runtime monitors such as turn limits and keyword filters to decide when a run should be stopped, upgraded, or assisted. However, these heuristics may stop runs that would otherwise succeed or allow failing runs to continue. To address this limitation, we introduce LeBet (Learn then Bet), a statistical learning framework that derives its learning objective from sufficient conditions for valid and powerful intervention. In particular, LeBet learns an interpretable OR-of-AND monitor and accumulates evidence through a fixed betting statistic, intervening when the evidence reaches a prescribed threshold. Under finite within-class exchangeability and leave-one-out stability, we derive finite-sample guarantees for false-positive control (validity) and detection power conditional on the training data, using the same trajectories for learning and calibration without assuming independent and identically distributed trajectories. To address the intractable combinatorial optimization problem in our learning formulation, we use stochastic local search that leverages the monitor's Boolean structure to propose rule edits aimed at improving empirical separation. On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, the learned monitor saves $34.46\%$ of input-plus-output tokens and increases output precision from $18.33\%$ to $21.59\%$. The empirical false-positive rate is $13.64\%$. Our results show how to formalize the learning problem over interpretable rule sets with statistical conditions and establish training-conditional guarantees for reliable intervention based on partial histories.

items.title: Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified? A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multimodal Time Series Forecasting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified? A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17680v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) systems increasingly combine sensed time series with external text such as expert reports and news, yet how reliably models use text that agrees or conflicts with the sensed history remains unclear. We introduce the first real-world diagnostic benchmark organized by text-history relationship: 1,762 text-window pairs across sensor telemetry (Weather), web-service traffic (Wikipedia), and market data streams (Finance), each labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified by whether the text's direction agrees with the historical trend, opposes it, or is not stated. Across ten pretrained models evaluated zero-shot, we investigate text selection and combination under text-history relationships (RQ1) and error diagnosis and horizon-scaled revision control (RQ2). For RQ1, we compare two types of text on paired Weather windows: one directly forecasts temperature changes, while the other describes related weather conditions, such as winds and fronts. Under Aligned, the first type yields the lowest error for most models. Under Conflicting, it increases most models' error above the no-text baseline; we therefore add only its stated magnitude and timing to the second type. Compared with either type alone, this combination lowers mean absolute scaled error (MASE) for six models and raises directional accuracy (DA) for seven. For RQ2, an error decomposition attributes the error increase to oversized revisions, and a training-free rule that limits them outperforms forecasts both with and without text for the four models with this trade-off, lowering MASE by 4.49%-21.98% and raising DA by 2.99%-9.71%. Our dataset is available at https://github.com/Shelton1202/ACU-Bench.

items.title: OCTAVE: A Capability-Resolved Benchmark for End-to-End HTML5 Game Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OCTAVE: A Capability-Resolved Benchmark for End-to-End HTML5 Game Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Complete game generation requires agents to coordinate rules, interactions, states, and presentation over a long development process. A single aggregate score obscures which capabilities are implemented and which requirements remain unmet. We present OCTAVE, a benchmark for complete HTML5 game generation organized around eight Capability Dimensions, with 180 tasks and 1,800 Evaluation Requirements drawn from real player requests, commercial-mechanics reconstruction, and human expert design. It covers PC Web, Mobile Web, 2D, and 3D. Requirements distinguish Completeness, assessing publicly specified core implementation, from Richness, assessing hidden, deeper system relationships. Static source-code judgments provide requirement-level diagnosis across capabilities and task conditions. Evaluation of 11 model-harness combinations yields 33.2% Completeness and 32.5% Richness; 19.9% of generation records are static gate failures or missing artifacts. Excluding same-model self-evaluation, even the best combination remains below 50% on both public and hidden requirements. Richness is not harder than Completeness under every task condition. Systems perform relatively better on Core Rules and Numerical Design, while AI/NPC and Feedback and Game Feel show more prominent gaps. Requirement difficulty offers coarse stratification but is only weakly negatively correlated with pass rates. A limited human cross-check finds that requirements judged satisfied by humans but failed by the automated evaluator are the main direction of disagreement. OCTAVE extends evaluation beyond aggregate scores to diagnosis localized by requirement, capability, and task condition.

items.title: Co-Sight Harness: Externalized Control Assets and Deterministic Enforcement for Long-Horizon Business Agents [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Co-Sight Harness: Externalized Control Assets and Deterministic Enforcement for Long-Horizon Business Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon business workflows fail in two ways: errors accumulate as a chain of activities lengthens, and the knowledge an activity needs is written in a different vocabulary from the user's request. We study whether such workflows can be made reliable without changing the language model. Our method keeps the backbone fixed and moves the workflow definition, state and domain knowledge into versioned control assets outside the model. A state machine and machine-checkable acceptance gates enforce these assets during execution; an independent auditor grades the resulting trace. The assets are updated only after a regression check and human approval .We evaluate the method on three deployed workflows exceeding 200 steps. On Domain A, a 120-case end-to-end evaluation set shows unattended completion rising from 50% to 100%, retrieval recall from 56% to 91.67%, and end-to-end latency dropping from 440 to 159 minutes, with scenario-analysis recall rising from 45% to 93%. Two other domains were taken over by teams that did not write the assets, one in four days and one in seven days. A controlled ablation separates the two failure sources. The code is available at https://github.com/ZTE-AICloud/Co-Sight/tree/master/Co-Sight%20Harness.

items.title: An AI-enabled high-resolution chlorophyll-a forecasting model that outperforms the operational global biogeochemical system [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: An AI-enabled high-resolution chlorophyll-a forecasting model that outperforms the operational global biogeochemical system
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17704v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Surface chlorophyll-a concentration is a key indicator of marine phytoplankton variability, and short-term forecasts of its distribution provide advance information for marine ecosystem monitoring and management. However, interactions between physical transport and biological processes complicate chlorophyll-a forecasting, and simulating these coupled processes with conventional numerical models imposes substantial computational demands. Here we introduce ChlCast, an AI model that generates daily forecasts of surface chlorophyll-a concentration over a 10-day horizon at approximately 4-km resolution between 60$^\circ$S and 60$^\circ$N. ChlCast combines factorized spatiotemporal convolutions with a multiscale architecture to learn from historical chlorophyll-a fields and climatological information. Compared with the operational 0.25$^\circ$ Copernicus global ocean biogeochemical forecasting system, ChlCast reduces mean absolute error and root mean square error by 70.74% and 47.63%, respectively, against satellite-derived Level-4 chlorophyll-a fields, and by 35.03% and 13.07% against independent BGC-Argo in situ observations. Coastal case studies further show that the 4-km forecasts retain coastal gradients and localized concentration maxima that are weakened by coarse-grid averaging. These results demonstrate the potential of observation-driven deep learning for high-resolution forecasting of surface chlorophyll-a variability at the near-global scale.

items.title: Cross-Linguistic Acoustic Biomarkers of Cognitive Impairment Across Interactive and Single-Speaker Speech Tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cross-Linguistic Acoustic Biomarkers of Cognitive Impairment Across Interactive and Single-Speaker Speech Tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17710v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multilingual dementia detection is essential for scalable and equitable screening. In recent years, automated speech analysis has emerged as a promising approach for supporting dementia detection by enabling non-invasive and scalable assessment of cognitive function. However, existing studies that use automated speech analysis often rely on one type of task, such as picture description, and use black-box models. These studies often neglect the role of task and language. To address these gaps, we performed a cross-linguistic and cross-task acoustic analysis that integrates a conversational dataset with structured speech tasks across four languages (Spanish, Mandarin, English, Japanese). We applied statistical, linguist-/clinician-guided, and machine learning model-based feature selection to derive compact acoustic feature sets while maintaining classification performance. This enabled systematic comparison of cognitive impairment-relevant features across datasets and tasks. Our results revealed that acoustic features did not generalize uniformly across tasks and languages. Temporal features remained robust across all datasets, consistently capturing timing disruption regardless of language or task. In contrast, speech rate showed strong task dependence -- emerging as informative mainly in single-speaker tasks with externally anchored content and pacing, but becoming less reliable when speech content was highly individualized. Pitch-related features further exhibited language-specific patterns, favoring chroma-related features in tonal languages (e.g., Mandarin) and F0-related features in non-tonal languages. These findings caution against indiscriminate pooling of heterogeneous speech data and underscore the need for interpretable, context-aware approaches to multilingual dementia detection using automated speech analysis.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17710v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multilingual dementia detection is essential for scalable and equitable screening. In recent years, automated speech analysis has emerged as a promising approach for supporting dementia detection by enabling non-invasive and scalable assessment of cognitive function. However, existing studies that use automated speech analysis often rely on one type of task, such as picture description, and use black-box models. These studies often neglect the role of task and language. To address these gaps, we performed a cross-linguistic and cross-task acoustic analysis that integrates a conversational dataset with structured speech tasks across four languages (Spanish, Mandarin, English, Japanese). We applied statistical, linguist-/clinician-guided, and machine learning model-based feature selection to derive compact acoustic feature sets while maintaining classification performance. This enabled systematic comparison of cognitive impairment-relevant features across datasets and tasks. Our results revealed that acoustic features did not generalize uniformly across tasks and languages. Temporal features remained robust across all datasets, consistently capturing timing disruption regardless of language or task. In contrast, speech rate showed strong task dependence -- emerging as informative mainly in single-speaker tasks with externally anchored content and pacing, but becoming less reliable when speech content was highly individualized. Pitch-related features further exhibited language-specific patterns, favoring chroma-related features in tonal languages (e.g., Mandarin) and F0-related features in non-tonal languages. These findings caution against indiscriminate pooling of heterogeneous speech data and underscore the need for interpretable, context-aware approaches to multilingual dementia detection using automated speech analysis.

items.title: Federated Soft Poly-Level Learning Over a Distributed Network with Guaranteed Convergence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Federated Soft Poly-Level Learning Over a Distributed Network with Guaranteed Convergence
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17722v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-level learning/optimization, e.g., bilevel optimization, has been recognized for its versatile applicability across a broad array of domains, spanning from signal processing to machine learning. However, most existing works focus on bilevel and trilevel optimization. In contrast, multi-level optimization problems involving four or more hierarchical levels, which we term poly-level learning (PLL) problems, remain largely unexplored.In addition, in practical PLL, data may be distributed across multiple nodes over a distributed network. Nevertheless, extant studies on PLL predominantly focus on the non-federated setting, necessitating the collection of data to central servers and thereby posing potential privacy risks. To this end, we propose a Federated Poly-Level Learning (FPLL) framework over a distributed network to tackle the PLL problems with soft constraints in a federated manner. FPLL hinges on a novel non-linear cut, i.e., $L$-cut, for the level-wise relaxation to the PLL problems. Additionally, the proposed federated algorithm is designed with adjustable parameters that allow for a flexible trade-off between its computational complexity and performance efficiency, enabling users to tune it according to specific application requirements. We also carry out non-asymptotic analysis to derive the iteration complexity for the proposed FPLL to achieve the $\epsilon$-Pareto stationary point. Extensive experiments have been undertaken to elucidate the superior efficacy of the proposed method.

items.title: A Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization in Model Merging [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization in Model Merging
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model merging constructs multi-task models without expensive joint training but often suffers from parameter interference. Some solutions mitigate this by constraining finetuning using data from the other tasks to be merged, violating the core independence and privacy assumption of model merging. Recent work offers preliminary empirical evidence that a universal, task-agnostic proxy distribution can substitute for such data, but leaves open when and why it suffices. To this end, we propose a \textit{Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization}, which characterizes the relationship between a proxy distribution and the distribution of other tasks to be merged through spectral coverage ($\alpha$) and leakage ($\beta$). Based on the framework, we derive a unified parameter interference bound: smaller $(\alpha, \beta)$ provably yields lower parameter interference through better spectral alignment. To exploit such a proxy, we augment the training objective with a proxy regularizer. Evaluating this regularizer during fine-tuning requires a concrete mechanism. We study three instantiations, including (J) an exact evaluation via Jacobian-vector products, (F) a frozen curvature approximation using the Fisher information matrix, and (O) an output-drift formulation that constrains the model's functional deviation on the proxy directly. We prove that all three coincide under the NTK linearization, where existing analyses of such regularizers stop, and go further to characterize standard non-linear fine-tuning, bounding how far each instantiation departs from its linearized reference and obtain a three-way hierarchy, zero for (J), proxy-independent for (F), and proxy-quality-scaling for (O). Empirical validation on the commonly used vision-language model CLIP confirms these theoretical predictions.

items.title: Knowledge After Collapse: Context and Wording Shape Factual Accessibility in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Knowledge After Collapse: Context and Wording Shape Factual Accessibility in Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a language model accepts a false correction in a factual discussion, its next answer can depend on how the conversation continues. We introduce Knowledge Answer Divergence (KAD), an event-conditioned evaluation protocol that distinguishes initial false-answer adoption from subsequent persistence, recovery, and abstention. KAD freezes the conversation at the first explicit adoption of a designated false target and branches independent probes from that exact history. This enables matched comparisons of post-adoption behavior and history-management interventions that a single susceptibility score cannot capture. We evaluate eight local checkpoint conditions and six hosted endpoints, alongside an audited 300-question rerun. In corrected Llama 3.2 Instruct 3B controls, a neutral-history branch yields 42/46 correct responses, compared with 16/46 under full history. A matched cue-placement control changes false adoption by 27.3 percentage points in Qwen 3.5 4B. Twelve independently authored pressure templates demonstrate substantial sensitivity to wording. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of KAD for evaluating factual reliability beyond initial susceptibility, enabling systematic comparisons of false-answer persistence, recovery conditions and conversational interventions.

items.title: Certified Improvements to Best-Known Thomson-Problem Configurations with a Search Pipeline Built with Large Language Model Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Certified Improvements to Best-Known Thomson-Problem Configurations with a Search Pipeline Built with Large Language Model Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Thomson problem asks for N unit charges on a sphere with minimum Coulomb energy; for large N the best configurations known are curated in the Cambridge Cluster Database, whose largest-N entries were set in October 2026. We report configurations for N = 912, 1382 and 2502 with energies 0.0036186, 0.0109730 and 0.0614033 below the database values, certified by exact integer arithmetic. All three are numerically strict local minima modulo rotations and keep the defect inventory and scar compositions of the database configurations; the database value for N = 912 had been reached by two different methods. Our search runs unconstrained replica-exchange basin hopping from the database configurations, with a shared pool of minima, recombination of improved regions after relabelling by geometry, and gradient-only polishing; replica-exchange basin hopping alone found the N = 912 and 1382 configurations, the former in one of five runs. We built and ran it with large language model agents (Claude, through a chat interface and the Claude Code agent), and we report every search, including those that failed. Two findings matter for others who search the database. Polishing alone lowers two entries by more than the threshold at which our pipeline reports a candidate, which produced two spurious records until candidates were compared with the polished database energies (the polished baseline). A local-relaxation speed-up passed its exactness test yet found nothing in a controlled comparison in which every arm with full relaxation went below the database value within 15 minutes. We distil three practices for computational discovery with large language model agents: calibrate the search code and verify candidates with code separate from the search, compare candidates with the polished baseline, and test design changes in controlled comparisons with pass criteria fixed in advance.

items.title: TReC: Evaluating Move-Induced State Changes in Instruction-Conditioned Go [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TReC: Evaluating Move-Induced State Changes in Instruction-Conditioned Go
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a Go model predicts a move different from the expert's, coordinate distance measures how far the prediction lands from the reference. We introduce Transition Representation Consistency (TReC) to compare how the two moves change a board-state embedding. Both moves are executed from the same position under the game rules, and TReC is the cosine similarity between the two resulting representation changes. In experiments with a frozen KataGo network on 680 mid-to-late-game positions from five games, the gap between the highest and lowest candidate per position has a median of 0.01 to 0.08 for the direct successor-state cosine and 0.88 to 1.33 for TReC, depending on the evaluator layer. TReC follows coordinate distance only weakly: the rank correlation between a candidate's distance to the reference and its TReC, computed within each position, has a median of -0.19 over these positions.

items.title: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is one of the most promising paths toward an AI singularity for superintelligence. Achieving this vision requires AI systems to undertake the full training pipeline for iterative improvement. Reinforcement learning (RL) plays an essential role in this cycle to improve model capabilities and generalization, yet automating RL remains difficult due to unstable training dynamics and the need for sustained supervision. We introduce AutoRL, a multi-agent system for automating RL training, as a cornerstone for future RSI. Different from conducting research by end-to-end complete experiments, AutoRL monitors the evolving training state and integrates process-level supervision and research into an ongoing RL training, following the practical workflow of an RL researcher. Specifically, AutoRL consists of three RL-specific agentic roles. Perceptors track training dynamics, rollouts, evaluation, and efficiency, triggering deliberation when they detect anomalies, degradation, or stagnation. Three complementary Proposers diagnose problems and refine candidate interventions through shared evidence and checks. The Orchestrator reviews their recommendation and applies approved changes through online hot updates or checkpoint-based resumption. Experiments on Qwen3 and LongCat-Flash-Lite demonstrate the superiority of AutoRL over static RL recipes and a general agent. The research records show that existing agents can handle unattended RL supervision and dynamic adjustment. The difficulty for future RSI lies in developing fundamental methods that are valuable for resource-consuming validation.

items.title: MASTARS: Multi-Agent Sequential Trajectory Augmentation with Return-Conditioned Subgoals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MASTARS: Multi-Agent Sequential Trajectory Augmentation with Return-Conditioned Subgoals
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The performance of offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is limited by the quality of the fixed offline dataset, motivating trajectory augmentation. However, augmenting multi-agent trajectories presents a fundamental challenge of the diversity-coordination trade-off: independent generation improves diversity but lacks coordination, while joint generation induces coordination but lacks diversity, reproducing the training distribution. To address this challenge in multi-agent data augmentation, we introduce MASTARS, a novel diffusion-based framework that generates multi-agent trajectories sequentially across agents while enforcing cross-agent consistent coordination via the method of inpainting. MASTARS produces trajectories that are diverse, coordinated and globally coherent. Experiments on various benchmarks such as MPE, SMAC, and SMAC-v2 demonstrate significant performance gains across multiple offline MARL methods.
